title: The Green Finance Paradox: Balancing Investment Risks, Financial Returns, and Environmental Sustainability in Emerging Economies
content: Green finance is promoted, in the same breath, as both a riskier and a safer place to put capital. Regulators warn that pushing credit toward environmental projects can raise a lender’s overall risk profile, because green assets are new, thinly documented and hard to collateralise; at the same time, a growing body of market evidence finds that green bonds trade at a persistent yield discount and that environmental, social and governance (ESG) equity portfolios often match or beat conventional benchmarks on a risk-adjusted basis. This paper calls that coexistence the green finance paradox and asks how it plays out, and can be resolved, in emerging economies, where the need for climate-aligned capital is greatest and the market infrastructure to price it is thinnest. We build an integrated conceptual framework that traces the paradox to four channels — information and asset immaturity, investor non-pecuniary preference, climate and transition risk pricing, and greenwashing or credibility risk — and we compile a comparative synthesis of risk-return evidence across green bonds, ESG equities and bank credit in developed and emerging markets. We then examine Uzbekistan and the wider Central Asian region as an illustrative case of a frontier green-finance market, drawing on its 2021 sovereign sustainability bond, 2023 sovereign and corporate green bond debuts, and early blended-finance partnerships with development banks. The synthesis shows that the paradox narrows, rather than disappears, as disclosure quality, secondary-market liquidity, blended de-risking instruments and policy credibility improve; under an illustrative moderate-to-optimistic policy scenario, these mechanisms can plausibly compress the emerging-market green risk premium by a magnitude comparable to the climate-related sovereign borrowing cost penalty documented in the literature. We conclude with recommendations for investors, banks and policymakers in emerging economies on sequencing taxonomy, guarantee and liquidity reforms so that environmental additionality and financial return are pursued as one objective rather than traded off against each other.
